note.question: Why would an innovator voluntarily give a proprietary technology to a direct rival, when will the rival actually adopt it to launch a new product, and who gains from the resulting multiproduct competition?
note.overview: The paper develops a sequential game in which one firm decides whether to share proprietary technology with a rival, the rival decides whether to adopt it and introduce a new product, and the firms then compete strategically in prices.

objects: Heterogeneous consumers distributed across three product-preference spokes
inputs: The model is complete information: product values, transfer rate, consumer distribution, and earlier sharing and adoption choices are known

decisions: Firm 1 shares or withholds its proprietary technology

Products are horizontally differentiated in a three-spoke market with uniformly distributed consumers and an outside option

components.label: Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium of sharing, adoption, pricing, and purchase
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium of sharing, adoption, pricing, and purchase. The paper solves simultaneous price Nash equilibria with and without product 3, then compares continuation profits to derive stage-1 sharing and adoption. Proposition 4 states that product 3 enters in equilibrium iff q_lower(theta)<=q<=q_upper(theta).

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Stage 1: firm 1 decides whether to share its technology; if it shares, firm 2 decides whether to adopt it and introduce product 3. Stage 2: the two firms simultaneously set the prices of their product portfolios. Stage 3: consumers choose among their available preferred products or the outside option. The game is solved by backward induction.
